summary: Describes using the HMAC construction with the SHA-1 hash as the authentication mechanism inside IPsec's ESP and AH. It parallels the HMAC-MD5 document with a different hash. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a secret handshake that computers use to prove a packet is real. This version uses a different scrambling recipe than its sibling document.

questions: why does hmac-sha-1-96 truncate to 96 bits
what key length does hmac-sha-1-96 use
subtitle: How IPsec uses HMAC with SHA-1, cut down to 96 bits, to prove a packet is genuine and unaltered.

tldr.problem: IPsec's ESP and AH need a keyed way to prove that a packet came from the expected sender and was not modified in transit.
tldr.mechanism: HMAC with the SHA-1 hash produces a 160-bit value. Only the first 96 bits are stored in the packet's authenticator field, and the receiver recomputes the value and compares those 96 bits. The key is always 160 bits.
tldr.outcome: It gives data origin authentication and integrity protection, as long as the secret key is shared only by the communicating parties. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 2404 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1998, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2404 specifies how to combine the SHA-1 hash with HMAC (defined in RFC 2104) as a keyed authentication mechanism inside the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and the Authentication Header (AH). The goal of HMAC-SHA-1-96 is to ensure that the packet is authentic and cannot be modified in transit.

HMAC is a secret key algorithm, so what it proves depends on who knows the key. If only the source and destination know the key, a correct HMAC proves that it must have been added by the source. That gives both data origin authentication and data integrity for packets exchanged between the two parties.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people share a secret. When a message arrives with the right secret mark, the receiver knows it came from the other person and was not changed.

sections.title: Algorithm and Mode
sections.content:
The SHA-1 algorithm is described in FIPS 180-1 and the HMAC algorithm in RFC 2104. HMAC is a framework into which various hashing algorithms, such as SHA-1, can be inserted. HMAC-SHA-1-96 operates on 64-byte blocks of data. Padding requirements are part of SHA-1 itself, so a SHA-1 built to FIPS 180-1 needs no additional padding, and no implicit packet padding is required for AH.

The algorithm produces a 160-bit authenticator value, which can be truncated as RFC 2104 describes. For ESP or AH, an implementation MUST support a truncated value that uses the first 96 bits.

  • On sending, the truncated value is stored in the authenticator field.
  • On receipt, the entire 160-bit value is computed and the first 96 bits are compared with the value in the authenticator field.
  • No other authenticator lengths are supported by HMAC-SHA-1-96.

The 96-bit length was chosen because it is the default authenticator length in AH and meets the security requirements of RFC 2104.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipe makes a long fingerprint, but only the first part is written on the packet. The receiver makes the whole fingerprint again and checks that the first part matches.

sections.title: Performance
sections.content:
The RFC quotes Bellare and colleagues: HMAC performance is essentially that of the underlying hash function. It adds that, at the time of writing, no detailed performance analysis had been done of SHA-1, HMAC, or HMAC combined with SHA-1.

RFC 2104 outlines an implementation modification that can improve per-packet performance without affecting interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding the secret mark costs about as much work as running the underlying scrambler once. There is also a known trick to make it a bit faster.

sections.title: Keying Material
sections.content:
HMAC-SHA-1-96 is a secret key algorithm. Although RFC 2104 specifies no fixed key length, for ESP or AH a fixed key length of 160 bits MUST be supported, and other key lengths MUST NOT be supported. The choice follows RFC 2104: keys shorter than the authenticator length weaken security, and longer keys do not significantly add strength.

A strong pseudo-random function MUST be used to generate the 160-bit key. No weak keys were specified for HMAC at the time of writing, though the RFC says this does not imply that none exist. If weak keys are ever identified, they must be rejected, followed by a request for replacement keys or a newly negotiated Security Association.

To give data origin authentication, the key distribution mechanism must make sure unique keys are allocated and are given only to the parties in the communication. The RFC also repeats the advice that periodic key refreshment is a fundamental security practice, even though current attacks do not point to a specific rekeying frequency. How keying material is obtained when one SA needs several keys is described in RFC 2401.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret must be exactly one size, must be made by a really good random-number maker, and must be shared with only the two people talking. Changing it every so often is also a good habit.

sections.title: Interaction with the ESP Cipher
sections.content: The RFC says that, as of writing, there are no known issues that prevent HMAC-SHA-1-96 from being used with any specific ESP cipher algorithm. In ESP, the authentication step is separate from the confidentiality mechanism, so it can sit beside whichever cipher is chosen.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret mark works no matter which secret code is used to hide the message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of HMAC-SHA-1-96 rests on the strength of HMAC and, to a lesser degree, the strength of SHA-1. At the time of writing there were no practical cryptographic attacks against it. The RFC notes that SHA-1 was never designed as a keyed hash, whereas HMAC had that goal from the start.

It cites RFC 2104: for a 64-byte block hash, a birthday attack involving the processing of 2^80 blocks would be infeasible unless the underlying hash were found to have collisions after 2^30 blocks, and a hash that weak would generally be considered unusable. Truncating the output may add security, and specifications that include HMAC are strongly encouraged to truncate.

Strength also depends on the correctness of the implementation, the key management mechanism, the secret key and every participating system. RFC 2202 provides test vectors and example code to help check HMAC-SHA-1-96 implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: As far as anyone knew then, nobody could fake the mark without the secret. It also matters that everyone builds the recipe correctly and keeps the secret safe.
